neighbours.label: infinitival 'to' introducing a purpose/result verb after a noun or adjective of sufficiency or means ('sufficient to [prove]', 'serve to', 'documents to support')
fire: The letters found in the desk were sufficient to convince the jury of his guilt.
A few short examples will serve to illustrate the difference between the two rules.
The plaintiff must provide enough evidence to support each part of the claim.
His careful notes were enough to show that the payments had been made on time.
The witnesses called by the defence failed to establish the custom they described.
One glance at the ledger is sufficient to reveal how badly the accounts were kept.
The committee gathered statistics to demonstrate that the policy had worked.
Several old maps were produced to prove where the boundary had once been drawn.
quiet: The letters found in the desk were sent to the jury before the trial began.
A few short examples were added at the end of the chapter on the two rules.
The plaintiff must deliver each document to the clerk of the court by Friday.
His careful notes were passed to the auditor after the payments had been made.
The witnesses called by the defence walked to the front of the courtroom slowly.
One copy of the ledger was returned to the owner after the inspection ended.
The committee sent its statistics to the minister in a sealed envelope.
Several old maps were given to the museum when the estate was settled.

notes: Card: ' to' is 23 of the top 32, in 'sufficient to convince', 'serve to place', 'documents to support'; output promotes demonstrative verbs (show, indicate, account, enable). Near misses use prepositional 'to' (direction/recipient) in the same legal/formal register.
